entry: Ethnic group mainly inhabiting the [[Arab world]] in West Asia and North Africa, with a significant diaspora elsewhere. Before the spread of Arabic in the wake of the Arab conquests, “Arab” largely referred to the Semitic inhabitants, both settled and nomadic, of the [[Arabian Peninsula]] and the Syrian Desert. In modern usage it includes people across the Greater Middle East who share Arabic as a native language. The Nabataean Arabs established a kingdom with [[Petra]] as its capital in classical antiquity, and the Palmyrene Empire under Queen Zenobia encompassed Egypt and large parts of Anatolia. At their peak, Arab territories stretched from southern France to western China. The [[Arab League]] was formed on March 22, 1945. About 93% of Arabs are [[Muslims]], with most of the rest Christian and smaller Druze and Baháʼí communities.

Family of [[Monocotyledon|monocotyledonous]] flowering plants, also known as the arum family, whose members are often called aroids. Flowers are borne on a spadix, usually accompanied by a spathe, a leaf-like bract. The family has 114 genera and about 3,750 known species, most diverse in the New World tropics and also distributed in the Old World tropics and northern temperate regions. Most species produce calcium oxalate crystals called raphides, which irritate the mouth and throat when raw vegetation is eaten. Many species are thermogenic, with flowers reaching up to 45 °C even when the surrounding air is much cooler, which helps attract [[Beetle|beetles]] or flies for pollination. Genera such as [[Anthurium]] and [[Philodendron]] are widely cultivated as ornamentals.

Class of [[Arthropod|arthropods]] in the subphylum Chelicerata, including [[Spider|spiders]], [[Scorpion|scorpions]], [[Tick|ticks]], [[Mite|mites]], pseudoscorpions, harvestmen and camel spiders. Almost all adults have eight legs, unlike adult [[Insect|insects]], which have six, and arachnids lack antennae and wings. Their body has two regions, the prosoma (cephalothorax) and the opisthosoma (abdomen), and the chelicerae serve in feeding and defense. Almost all living arachnids are terrestrial, although some inhabit freshwater and marine environments. They comprise over 110,000 named species, of which 51,000 are spiders. The term derives from the Greek *aráchnē*, meaning ‘spider’, from the myth of the weaver Arachne, who was turned into a spider.

Former endorheic salt lake between [[Kazakhstan]] and [[Uzbekistan]], once the fourth-largest lake in the world, with an area of 68,000 sq km (26,300 sq mi). It began shrinking in the 1960s after Soviet irrigation projects diverted the rivers that fed it, principally the [[Amu Darya]] and [[Syr Darya]]. By 2007 it had declined to 10% of its original size, and by August 2014 its eastern basin had completely dried up, becoming the Aralkum Desert. The name, from Mongolic and Turkic languages, means “Sea of Islands” for the more than 1,100 islands that once dotted its waters. A dam completed in 2005 raised water levels in the North Aral Sea, and fish returned in sufficient numbers for some fishing by 2013. United Nations secretary general Ban Ki-moon called the shrinking “one of the planet’s worst environmental disasters”.

Northwest Semitic language that originated in the ancient region of Syria and spread to [[Mesopotamia]], the [[Levant|southern Levant]] and beyond. Aramaic has been written and spoken in different varieties for over 3,000 years. It was the language of public life and administration in the [[Neo-Assyrian Empire]], the Neo-Babylonian and [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid]] empires, and it remains a language of worship in [[Christianity]] and Gnosticism. Its alphabet, derived from the Phoenician alphabet, became the base for the [[Hebrew alphabet]] and the [[Arabic alphabet]]. Early inscriptions date from the 11th century BC. Aramaic is considered endangered, and its modern eastern branch is spoken by Assyrians, Mandeans and a small contingent of Mizrahi Jews. Most historians believe it was the primary language spoken by [[Jesus]] in preaching and everyday life.

Genus of large, air-breathing bonytongue [[Fish|fishes]] native to the Amazon and Essequibo basins of South America. *Arapaima* is among the world’s largest freshwater fishes, reaching as much as 3 m (9.8 ft) in length. Its swim bladder is modified into a lung-like organ, which allows it to breathe air. It is an important food fish that has declined in its native range due to overfishing and habitat loss. Taxonomy is unsettled: FishBase recognizes four species, and evidence suggests a fifth, *A. arapaima*, is the widespread species otherwise included in *A. gigas*. Introduced populations outside the native range are sometimes considered [[Invasive species|invasive]]. Arapaima escaped from [[Aquaculture|aquaculture]] ponds in [[Kerala]], India, after floods in 2018. Its Portuguese name, pirarucu, derives from the Tupi words *pira* and *urucum*, meaning “red fish”.

Triumphal arch in Paris, France, at the western end of the Champs-Élysées. Commissioned by [[Napoleon]] in 1806 to honor those who fought and died for France in the [[French Revolution|French Revolutionary]] and Napoleonic Wars, it was designed by Jean-François Chalgrin and completed in 1836 under [[Louis Philippe I]]. Beneath its vault lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier from [[World War I]]. The arch is 49.54 m (162.5 ft) high and 44.82 m (147.0 ft) wide.

Coin-operated entertainment machine typically installed in public businesses such as restaurants, bars and amusement arcades. Most arcade games are primarily games of skill, and include arcade video games, [[Pinball|pinball machines]], electro-mechanical games, redemption games and merchandisers. Arcade video games were first introduced in the early 1970s, with Pong the first commercially successful game. Electro-mechanical games combined mechanical actions with electrical components such as motors, switches and relays, and included early light gun games. Merchandiser games, such as claw crane and coin pusher games, let the player win a prize through physical action with the machine. [[Pachinko]] is used mainly as a gambling device, filling a Japanese niche comparable to that of the [[Slot machine|slot machine]] in Western gambling. The 1983 [[Video game|video game]] crash reduced the dominance of arcades as home consoles grew.

Curved vertical structure spanning an open space underneath it. Arches may support the load above them or serve a purely decorative role. Decorative arches date to the 4th millennium BC, but load-bearing arches became popular only after the Romans adopted them, as in the [[Colosseum]]. Compared with a lintel, an arch can span a greater distance with the same amount of material, carry more weight, and be built from smaller, more manageable pieces, especially in [[Masonry|masonry]] construction. Arches also support many types of vault, and the barrel vault is a continuous arch. The role of arches in construction diminished in the mid-19th century with the introduction of [[Wrought iron|wrought iron]] and later [[Steel|steel]], whose high tensile strength made long lintels possible.

Recurring assemblage of artifact types, buildings and monuments from a specific period and region, which may constitute the material remains of a particular past human society. Whether it can be interpreted in terms of ethnic or political groups is often subject to long-unresolved debates. V. Gordon Childe described recurring pots, implements, ornaments, burial rites and house forms as a “cultural group”, which he assumed was the material expression of “a people”. Such cultures are usually named after the site where they were first defined, as with the [[Clovis culture]], or after an artifact type, as with the Linear Pottery culture. Critics argue that cultural taxonomies lack a strong consensus on their epistemological aims, and archaeological cultures were at times equated with separate peoples, leading in some cases to nationalist archaeologies.

Exposure, processing and recording of archaeological remains at a site, or “dig”, which may be studied over a few weeks to several years. Excavation recovers artifacts, features such as post molds, [[Burial|burials]] and hearths, ecofacts such as animal bones, pollen or charcoal, and archaeological context. Before digging, non-intrusive [[Remote sensing|remote sensing]], such as ground-penetrating radar, can indicate whether remains are present. Archaeologists often use [[Stratigraphy|stratigraphic]] excavation, removing a site one layer at a time to keep the timeline of material remains consistent. Recording is digital, and ideally the data should suffice to reconstruct the site in three-dimensional space. One of the first known excavations took place in the sixth century BC, when Nabonidus, king of Babylon, dug up a temple floor. Research excavation is carried out when time and resources allow a full exposure, while development-led excavation, usually funded by developers, is limited to the areas threatened by building.

Extinct genus of bird-like [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] that lived in the Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago. The name derives from Ancient Greek words meaning “ancient” and “feather, wing”. It lived in what is now southern Germany, when Europe was an [[Archipelago|archipelago]] in a shallow tropical sea, and it was about the size of a Eurasian magpie. Despite its [[Feather|feathers]] and inferred ability to fly or glide, it shared many features with small dromaeosaurid and troodontid dinosaurs, including sharp teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. Fourteen body fossils have been found, all from [[Limestone|limestone]] deposits near Solnhofen, Germany, and most preserve feather impressions. A complete specimen announced in 1861 came just two years after [[Charles Darwin]] published [[On the Origin of Species]], and the genus has since become key evidence for the origin of birds. Recent discoveries of other small feathered dinosaurs have raised questions about which animals are the ancestors of modern birds.

Second-lowest rank of angel, in a hierarchy put forward by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite in the 5th or 6th century. The Bible uses the term twice, both times for [[Michael (archangel)|Michael]] in the New Testament. In many offshoots of [[Judaism]], the highest-ranking angels, including Michael, Raphael, Gabriel and Uriel, are given the title *śārīm* (“princes”). Michael and [[Gabriel]] are recognized as archangels in Judaism and [[Islam]] and by most Christians. Raphael is also recognized in the Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and Eastern Orthodox churches. Islam names Jibra’il, Mika’il, Israfil and Malak Al-Mawt, the angel of death, as its archangels.

Austrian archduke and heir presumptive to the throne of [[Austria-Hungary]]. Eldest son of Archduke Karl Ludwig and nephew of Emperor [[Franz Joseph I]], he became heir presumptive in 1896. His marriage in 1900 to Sophie Chotek, a lady-in-waiting, was morganatic and was allowed only after he renounced his descendants’ right to the throne. In 1913 he was appointed inspector general of the Austro-Hungarian armed forces. His assassination in [[Sarajevo]] by [[Gavrilo Princip]] led to the July Crisis and was the most immediate cause of [[World War I]].

Second of the four geologic eons of Earth’s history, spanning 4,031 to 2,500 million years ago, between the [[Hadean]] and the Proterozoic. Earth was mostly a water world, with continental crust largely under a superocean deeper than today’s oceans. The atmosphere was a reducing atmosphere rich in methane and lacking free oxygen. The earliest known life, mostly shallow-water microbial mats called stromatolites, remained simple prokaryotes throughout the eon. Early [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]] carried out [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] in the mid-to-late Archean, causing a permanent chemical change in the ocean and atmosphere after the eon.

Sport, practice or skill of using a bow to shoot arrows at a target, historically used for hunting and combat. The word derives from the Latin *arcus*, meaning “bow”. The oldest known arrows, from South African sites such as Sibudu Cave, date to about 72,000 to 60,000 years ago, while the earliest complete bows and arrows come from northern Europe. Bows eventually replaced the spear-thrower as the main means of launching shafted projectiles on every continent except Australasia. The composite bow was likely invented in central Asia, and the Welsh longbow proved its worth in continental warfare at the Battle of Crécy. [[Crossbow|Crossbows]] were introduced in Europe around the tenth century. Gunpowder rendered bows obsolete in battle by the 16th century, after which archery became mainly a competitive sport and recreational activity.

Law of [[Fluid mechanics|fluid mechanics]] stating that the upward buoyant force on a body immersed in a fluid, fully or partially, equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. Formulated by [[Archimedes]] of Syracuse, it was set out in *On Floating Bodies* (c. 246 BC). It allows the buoyancy of any floating object to be calculated: the object rises if the net force is positive, sinks if negative, and stays in place if zero. The buoyant force equals fluid density multiplied by submerged volume and gravitational acceleration, written F = ρgV. It explains the flotation of ships and submarines.

Hydraulic machine consisting of an outer cylinder and an inner cylinder with helical blades. It can operate as a pump or a power generator, and has been used for drainage, [[Irrigation|irrigation]] and sewage management. Its origins are unclear. [[Archimedes]] is traditionally credited with inventing it, but other historians argue that the Egyptians were already using the screw, and the earliest mention dates from between 250 and 220 BC. Modern screw pumps are used in wastewater treatment plants. Run in reverse, screw turbines act as small hydroelectric generators at low-head sites, operating at flows of 0.01 m³/s to 14.5 m³/s and heads of 0.1 m to 10 m.

Chain, cluster or collection of islands, in an ocean, a sea or a smaller body of water. The word derives from the Italian *arcipelago*, a name for the [[Aegean Sea]] that was later applied to the Aegean Islands. Archipelagos may be oceanic islands formed by volcanic activity, such as the [[Hawaiian Islands]]; continental fragments cut off from a landmass; or continental islands that still sit on the [[Continental shelf|continental shelf]], such as the [[Arctic Archipelago|Canadian Arctic Archipelago]]. Coral cay archipelagos form when currents build up sediments on coral reefs. The Archipelago Sea in [[Finland]] has approximately 40,000 islands, and [[Indonesia]] is the largest archipelagic state, with more than 17,500 islands and about 284 million people.

[[Technical drawing]] of a building or building project, used to develop a design, communicate it to clients and builders, guide construction or record an existing building. Drawings follow conventions for views such as floor plans and sections, sheet sizes, units, scales and annotation. A floor plan is a horizontal section cut through a building at about 1.2 meters (four feet) above floor level. Drawings are made to scale so that dimensions can be read from them, and the note “Do not scale off dimensions” guards against copying errors. Drawings were once made in ink and copied by hand, and in the 20th century they moved to tracing paper for mechanical copying. Most architectural drawings are now made with [[Computer|computer]]-aided design (CAD) software.

Discipline that deals with the engineering and construction of buildings, including environmental, structural, mechanical, electrical and computational systems. Also called building engineering, it is distinguished from [[Interior design|interior design]] and architectural design. Architectural engineers focus on structural integrity, mechanical systems and energy efficiency, and collaborate with architects. Mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) specialists design heating, ventilation and air conditioning, [[Plumbing|plumbing]], electric power distribution and [[Lighting|lighting]]. Structural engineering analyzes buildings, bridges and towers against loads such as wind, rain, ice and seismic forces. Emerging as a licensed profession in the 20th century, the field addresses greenhouse gas emissions and the construction of resilient buildings.

Act of thinking, discussing and writing about [[Architecture|architecture]]. It is taught in architecture schools and takes forms such as the lecture, the treatise and the competition entry. The Roman writer [[Vitruvius]] produced the most prominent surviving theory of antiquity in *De architectura*, probably written between 27 and 23 BC, which defined the classical orders and proposed three laws: *firmitas*, *utilitas* and *venustas*, translated in the 17th century as “firmness, commodity, and delight.” Its rediscovery in 1414 influenced Renaissance architects such as [[Leon Battista Alberti]]. Books, magazines and journals published an unprecedented number of works by architects and critics in the 20th century, so that styles and movements formed and dissolved more quickly than before.

Architectural traditions rooted in the history, culture and religion of [[India]]. Hindu, Jain, Buddhist and Sikh styles are the most prevalent, alongside Indo-Islamic, Rajput, Mughal, South Indian and Indo-Saracenic architecture. Early wooden structures did not survive, so the earliest surviving examples are rock-cut temples. Hindu temples are traditionally divided into the Dravidian style of southern India and the Nagara style of northern India, with regional variations. The [[Delhi Sultanate]] developed Indo-Islamic architecture, which the [[Mughal Empire]] brought to its height, with the [[Taj Mahal]] as its high point. British colonial rule introduced Neoclassical and Gothic Revival styles, which merged with Indo-Islamic forms into the Indo-Saracenic style. After independence, Swiss-French architect [[Le Corbusier]] was commissioned to design the city of [[Chandigarh]], which influenced a generation of architects toward modernism.

Ancient architectural style of the Tigris–Euphrates river region, spanning from the 10th millennium BC, when the first permanent structures were built, to the 6th century BC. Its cultures included the [[Sumer|Sumerians]], Akkadians, [[Assyria|Assyrians]] and [[Babylon|Babylonians]]. Its accomplishments included [[Urban planning|urban planning]], the courtyard house and ziggurats, and scribes drafted and managed construction for government, nobility or royalty. Brick was the ordinary building material, and Sumerian masonry was usually mortarless. Buildings were periodically destroyed and rebuilt on the same spot, raising the level of cities into mounds. Civic buildings protected their facades with cones of colored stone, terracotta panels and clay nails. Babylonian temples were massive structures of crude brick supported by buttresses, and Assyria imitated this brick architecture in its own palaces and temples. Prized imports included cedar from [[Lebanon]].

Accumulation of historical records or materials in any medium, or the facility in which they are kept. Archives contain primary source documents that accumulate over an individual’s or organization’s lifetime, generated naturally through legal, commercial, administrative or social activity and kept to show that history and function. Archival records are usually unpublished and often unique, unlike books. Records are selected for permanent preservation for their enduring cultural, historical or evidentiary value, and the choice of what to include can be a political act. Clay-tablet archives from the third and second millennia BC have been found at [[Ebla]], [[Ugarit]] and other sites. A person who works in archives is an archivist, and the field is called archival science. Archives are distinct from [[Library|libraries]], although archival collections are often housed within library buildings.
